power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Volunteers were recruited from participant databases of the TU Dresden and the Max-Planck-Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences, and via local advertising in the Leipzig and Dresden areas.

Participants were excluded if they reported any current neurological or psychiatric condition, took psychotropic medication, or scored below 23 during onsite Montreal Cognitive Assessment (17) testing (for older adults).
All participants (and caregivers where applicable) provided written informed consent and were compensated for their time.
Participants are instructed to try to earn as many and lose as few points as possible.

The first four trials of each game are forced-choice trials in which participants are directed to play specific bandits: sometimes in a [2, 2] choice pattern, so that each bandit is encountered equally often and are thus equally informative, sometimes in a [1, 3] or [3, 1] choice pattern, so that one bandit is encountered less often and is thus more informative than the other.

Further in line with prior work (7), participants were overall more likely to choose the more informative bandit in the losses compared to the gains condition (Figure 2-A), as reflected in an interaction between information difference and motivational context (β=-.68, z=-10.55, p<.0001).

In the Leipzig sample, participants were also specifically excluded if they were over-or underweight, pregnant or breast-feeding, color vision deficient, if they had (first-degree family history) of epilepsy or schizophrenia, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, dyslexia, any present and past psychiatric disorder (except specific phobias) ascertained using the German version of the SCID. text.text: Navigating an uncertain world, we constantly face the explore-exploit dilemma: should we stick with what we know, or explore options that may or may not prove better?
An influential theory proposes that humans solve this dilemma through a division of labor in time: explore in childhood, exploit in old age.
Our work adds critical empirical nuance to this theory.

Exploration can manifest as deliberate information-seeking ("directed exploration") or choice randomness ("random exploration"), and these strategies are employed differently for gain-seeking and loss-avoidance.
Here, we ask how these modes of exploration relate to one another and jointly shape decision-making across the lifespan.
A cross-sectional sample of 254 participants aged 8-79 performed a bandit task dissociating directed and random exploration in gain-seeking and lossavoidance contexts.

Factor analysis revealed three factors driving behavior: two domain-specific factors reflecting information-seeking for gains and loss-avoidance, respectively, and a domain-general factor reflecting choice randomness.

Directed exploration for gains increased steadily and well into young adulthood before declining in older adulthood, whereas directed exploration for loss-avoidance changed little across the lifespan.
Children and older adults, relative to young adults, were characterized by greater choice randomness across contexts, even when exploration was disadvantageous.
Though working memory and processing speed accounted for some of these effects, independent effects of age remained.

Our findings demonstrate that exploration is not a unitary phenomenon: it encompasses dissociable subprocesses -some domain-specific and others domain-general -with distinct developmental timelines that are shaped by cognitive maturation and decline as well as factors beyond cognitive ability.
When navigating an uncertain world, we face a fundamental dilemma: should we stick with what we know, or explore options that may or may not prove better?
The response may be different depending on our stage of life and whether we are motivated by gainseeking or loss-avoidance.

In participants aged 8 to 79, deliberate information-seeking to maximize gains increased steadily from childhood into young adulthood before declining in old age, whereas information-seeking to avoid losses remained relatively stable throughout life.
Across contexts, children and older adults were also less strategic, choosing at random even when exploring unfamiliar options was disadvantageous.
Our findings show that exploration encompasses domain-specific and domain-general subprocesses that develop according to their own timelines.
The explore-exploit-dilemma is a fundamental challenge of adaptive decision-making at every stage of the human lifespan.

A prominent theory by Gopnik and colleagues (1) proposes that we partially solve this dilemma through a "division of labor in time", i.e., by exploring during childhood and exploiting what we have learned during adulthood and older age.

text.text: Though compelling, this account is complicated by two intersecting strands of research.
The first shows that not all exploration is created equal.

Among others, there is directed exploration, where choices are deliberately biased towards informative options, and random exploration, where random choice behavior facilitates information gain by chance (2).

text.text: Likewise, exploration can be employed non-strategically or strategically -if and when the environment offers sufficient opportunity to capitalize on acquired information (2).

text.text: It can be driven by factors such as novelty (3, 4), uncertainty (5), boredom (6), and the "richness" of the environment (i.e., availability of reward) (7, 8).

text.text: The second strand shows that these different kinds of exploration have divergent developmental trajectories.

Thus, in line with Gopnik and colleagues' theory, several studies report that children and adolescents have an increased tendency to seek out uncertainty (4, 9, 10) and to engage in random or value-free exploration (3-5), while older adults have been shown to display diminished uncertainty seeking and random exploration (11, 12).

text.text: However, novelty seeking seems to remain stable at least across early-life development (3, 4), and strategic directed exploration has been demonstrated to expand rather than recede during adolescence (13), consistent with increasingly sophisticated cognitive abilities.

text.text: Understanding the development of exploration therefore does not mean tracking a unidimensional behavior from childhood to old age.
Rather, it means identifying independent and interacting components that result in (different) explorative behavior(s) in different contexts, and investigating their impact across the lifespan.

In this study, we contribute to a better understanding of exploratory behavior from a lifespan perspective by studying several facets of exploration in a large in-lab sample spanning childhood and adolescence as well as young adulthood and old age.

We investigate exploration along three dimensions and their intersections -strategic vs non-strategic, random vs directed, and motivated by gains or loss-avoidance -using the Horizon task, a bandit task designed to independently manipulate the value and informativeness of different options, the future value of information, and the motivational context (2, 7).

text.text: In line with previous findings, we hypothesize that in the gains domain, strategic exploration, especially strategic directed exploration, would expand from childhood to adulthood (13), while randomness would decline (5), with both reaching a plateau in young adulthood.
We further hypothesize that older age would be associated with less directed and strategic random exploration (11, 12).

text.text: As illustrated in Fig. 1-B, the task consists of two blocks of 80 games each, a gains and a loss block.

text.text: In each game, participants choose between two slot machines (one-armed bandits) with either 5 or 10 slots (trials).
Each choice is followed by feedback (point gains in gains block, point losses in loss block).
Participants are instructed to try to earn as many and lose as few points as possible.
Payoffs for each bandit are drawn from normal distributions with variable means and a fixed standard deviation (SD=8).
The task has several key manipulations to independently vary the value and informativeness of the bandits, as well as the strategic utility of exploration.
First, the task systematically manipulates the value difference between bandits.

That is, in each game, the mean payoff of one bandit (chosen at random) is set to either 40 or 60 (-40 or -60 in the loss block), and the mean of the other bandit is offset relative to that value by ±30, ±20, ±12, ±8, or ±4.
Second, the task manipulates the informativeness of the bandits independent of their values.

The first four trials of each game are forced-choice trials in which participants are directed to play specific bandits: sometimes in a [2, 2] choice pattern, so that each bandit is encountered equally often and are thus equally informative, sometimes in a [1, 3] or [3, 1] choice pattern, so that one bandit is encountered less often and is thus more informative than the other.
text.formatted: The first four trials of each game are forced-choice trials in which participants are directed to play specific bandits: sometimes in a <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref> choice pattern, so that each bandit is encountered equally often and are thus equally informative, sometimes in a <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref> or <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1]</ref> choice pattern, so that one bandit is encountered less often and is thus more informative than the other.

text.text: Third, the task manipulates the strategic utility of exploration for future choices by varying the number of free choice trials after the first four (forced-choice) trials (the horizon).
Exploration on the first free-choice trial is useful only if that information can be used in the future: in games with 5 trials in total (short horizon), the first free choice trial is also the last.
In this situation, a rational strategic agent should always exploit (i.e., choose the bandit with the higher observed mean reward value).
In games with 10 trials in total, the first free choice trial is one out of six (long horizon), so that it may make sense to explore.

As Wilson et al. have previously shown (2), humans do this by preferentially choosing more informative bandits in the long horizon (strategic directed exploration) but also by choosing more randomly (less driven by value) , which promotes information gain through more balanced sampling of bandits (strategic random exploration).
Note that a subset of participants (N=16) performed 160 games per block.
Due to time constraints, this was reduced to 80 games per block in subsequent participants; all games are retained in the analysis.

To analyze behavior on the first free choice trial of each game, we employed a logistic mixed-effects model with maximal random effects structure (20) estimated using fitglme in MATLAB 2023a: The coefficient for Information difference (β Δinfo ) captures the tendency to choose the bandit with higher informativeness, i.e., directed exploration.
The coefficient for Value difference (β Δvalue ) captures the tendency to exploit the higher mean bandit, i.e., random exploration, reverse coded.

Their respective interactions with horizon capture the strategic deployment of information-seeking and random decision-making in long horizon games (strategic directed and random exploration, respectively).
Note that we do not include the Motivational context x Block interaction (order effect).

This is because, due to problems with randomization in the Dresden sample, 80% of participants performed the loss condition first, including all children (8) (9) (10) (11) (12) and older adults (65+), and therefore age and order are partially confounded.

To better understand the relationships between directed and random, strategic and non-strategic exploration for gains and loss-avoidance respectively, we performed exploratory factor analysis on the random slopes from M1 for Information difference (β Δinfo ) and Value difference (β Δvalue ) in short and long horizon games and the gains and losses conditions.

Because these are linear combinations of predictors (main effects and interactions), we calculate their variance as a function of the predictor variances and their covariances as 𝑳 × 𝚺 ̂× 𝑳 ⊤ (21), where 𝑳 is the contrast matrix of the predictors and 𝚺 ̂ is the variance-covariance matrix of M1.
We calculated the resulting matrix' eigenvalues and used the scree plot and Kaiser criterion to determine the appropriate number of factors.
We then performed factor analysis with Promax rotation (i.e., oblique rotation allowing for correlated factors) using the factoran function in MATLAB 2023a.

text.text: Exploration is not a unitary phenomenon (2, 4, 6, 7).

text.text: A central distinction is between directed exploration, where people explicitly seek out unfamiliar options, and random exploration, where they inject randomness into their response pattern to "passively" increase sampling of unfamiliar options (2).
The motivational context -whether the focus is on maximizing gains or avoiding losses -has been shown to modulate how we employ these strategies (7).

text.text: In this study, a large sample of participants with an age range spanning from childhood to old age performed a gain-and loss-framed variant of the Horizon task (7), allowing us to characterize how strategies of exploration for gain and loss-avoidance change across the lifespan.
First, we replicate previous findings, confirming that people strategically use random exploration in both gain-seeking and loss-avoidance contexts (7).
text.formatted: First, we replicate previous findings, confirming that people strategically use random exploration in both gain-seeking and loss-avoidance contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: We also confirm that in loss-avoidance contexts, participants tend to seek out unfamiliar options even when information has no strategic value (7).
text.formatted: We also confirm that in loss-avoidance contexts, participants tend to seek out unfamiliar options even when information has no strategic value <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Extending prior work, we show that in gainseeking contexts, participants tended to avoid unfamiliar options when information had no strategic value but overcame this bias when information was useful, demonstrating strategic directed exploration (2, 7).
text.formatted: Extending prior work, we show that in gainseeking contexts, participants tended to avoid unfamiliar options when information had no strategic value but overcame this bias when information was useful, demonstrating strategic directed exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7)</ref>.

text.text: There was no evidence of a strategic deployment of directed exploration in loss-avoidance contexts when the whole sample was considered, although exploratory analyses in young adults replicated Krueger et al.-'s (7) finding of strategic directed exploration of loss avoidance (see Supplement for details).
We further demonstrate that individual tendencies towards directed and random exploration across motivational contexts were largely independent of each other.
This was further underscored by divergent and distinct associations with age and cognitive abilities.

First, exploratory factor analyses leveraging the variance-covariance structure of our behavioral model identified three mostly independent factors: one dominated by value sensitivity across horizons and conditions (Exploitation); and two factors reflecting directed exploration in the gains and loss-avoidance conditions, respectively.
The three factors were only weakly correlated.
Exploitation had a small negative association with Information seeking for gains and none with Information seeking for loss-avoidance.

Thus, a person's inclination towards exploitation -the mirror image of their inclination towards random exploration -reveals almost nothing about their inclination toward directed exploration, consistent with previous reports of different neural substrates (23).

text.text: Similarly, Information seeking for gains and loss-avoidance were effectively orthogonal.
The latter is consistent with prior investigations indicating that individual differences in uncertainty processing are mostly independent across motivational contexts (24, 25).

text.text: Distinct developmental timelines of directed exploration for gains and loss-avoidance
In line with the factor analysis, our data suggest that directed exploration for gains and losses, and random exploration develop according to different age trajectories.
Thus, directed exploration for gains and loss-avoidance showed noticeably divergent relationships with age.
Consistent with previous work (13, 26), strategic directed exploration for gains increased steadily, substantially, and well into young adulthood.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26)</ref>, strategic directed exploration for gains increased steadily, substantially, and well into young adulthood.

text.text: Strategic directed exploration for loss-avoidance also expanded, though much less precipitously.
The pattern reversed in older adults, who, in line with prior work (11, 12), showed a decline of strategic directed exploration in the gains and the losses condition relative to younger adults.
text.formatted: The pattern reversed in older adults, who, in line with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12)</ref>, showed a decline of strategic directed exploration in the gains and the losses condition relative to younger adults.

text.text: The divergence across conditions is reminiscent of prior reports that another behavior involving uncertainty processing -risk-taking -, shows more pronounced age-related changes in the gains than the losses domain (27, 28).
text.formatted: The divergence across conditions is reminiscent of prior reports that another behavior involving uncertainty processing -risk-taking -, shows more pronounced age-related changes in the gains than the losses domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref>.

text.text: To understand what drives the divergence, it helps to disentangle different mechanistic contributions.
Recall that the gain-loss divergence from childhood to young adulthood reflected two parallel processes.

First, strategic directed exploration -the additional premium placed on information in long-horizon games -expanded with age across conditions; second, the overall tendency to choose the more informative bandit increased with age in the gains, but not the losses condition.
These effects compounded, such that the rise of the premium on information was particularly sharp in long horizon games of the gains condition.

Interestingly, accounting for age-related improvements in working-memory completely absorbed the gain/loss, but not the horizon differences in the age-related expansion of directed exploration, which remained statistically significant.
This suggests that the influences of age and cognitive improvements are partially independent from each other.

In fact, mediation analyses showed that -ceteris paribus -working memory and age had opposing directional effects on directed exploration in the loss domain: highe r working memory was associated with weaker, and age with stronger preference for more informative bandits in the loss condition.

This suggests that two opposing developmental processes might underlie the observed pattern of age effects on directed exploration: from childhood to young adulthood, age-related gains in cognitive abilities may diminish deviations from rationality, reducing a tendency toward familiarity-seeking in the gains condition and toward ambiguity-seeking in the loss condition.
An independent maturational process could, at the same time, lead to an overall expansion in strategic information seeking.

Speculatively, this could reflect the increasing real-world strategic utility of information during young or "emerging" adulthood: the time period between age 18 and 29, defined by consequential, sometimes irreversible decisions about career commitments, relationships, family planning and so on (29).
text.formatted: Speculatively, this could reflect the increasing real-world strategic utility of information during young or "emerging" adulthood: the time period between age 18 and 29, defined by consequential, sometimes irreversible decisions about career commitments, relationships, family planning and so on <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>.

text.text: It is arguably during this period that gathering information before committing has the greatest value.
Whether this manifests when informationseeking is tested in the lab is speculative, but the alignment in developmental timing is suggestive.
Older adults showed diminished sensitivity to information compared to younger adults and adolescents in the gains condition.

Interestingly, accounting for neuropsychological metrics did not abolish this effect, indicating that in the older age group, there might be a "genuinely" age-related difference in directed exploration in different motivational contexts.

A speculative interpretation might invoke Carstensen's socioemotional sensitivity theory (30), which posits that as perceived future time horizon shrinks in old age, motivation shifts toward more present and consumption focused goals, such that future-relevant information is discounted in favor of more certain, proximate gains.

text.text: In contrast to what we saw for directed exploration and in line with the factor analysis, there was no difference in the development of random exploration for gains and lossavoidance.
Strategic random exploration expanded rapidly during childhood and reached a plateau in late adolescence, where the difference in choice randomness across horizons reached its maximum.

Critically, this was largely driven by increasing sensitivity to value differences between bandits in short horizon games -which makes people more likely to exploit when exploration is strategically inadvisable -rather than decreasing value sensitivity in long horizon games.
This finding dovetails with a welldocumented overall decrease in choice randomness in adolescence (5, 14, 16, 31, 32).
Congruently, the age-related increase in value sensitivity was mediated by processing speed, a measure of general cognitive efficiency.

The mirror image of this pattern emerged in later life: older adults showed less strategic random exploration than younger adults, again mostly due to maladaptively high randomness in shorthorizon games rather than lower long horizon randomness.
As in the younger cohort, the difference in value sensitivity disappeared when processing speed was controlled for.

Though contrary to previous reports emphasizing reduced strategic random exploration in aging (11, 12), these findings chime with studies showing an overall increase in choice randomness (33, 34) and fluid intelligence (35) in older age.

text.text: Together, our data suggest that the development of random exploration is primarily driven by the acquisition and subsequent erosion of value sensitivity and general cognitive efficiency, rather than by bona fide changes of the disposition to explore.

An intriguing possibility is that "random exploration" may in fact be better construed as "strategic exploitation", where the cognitive resources needed for precise value-driven decision-making are deployed when it is useful to do so -if and when those resources are available.

Future work should investigate whether this is related to developmental changes in (striatal) dopamine and noradrenaline signaling, both of which have been implicated in general cognitive functioning across the lifespan (36) (37) (38), choice randomness in exploration contexts (39) (40) (41) (42) (43), and indeed, the willingness to exert cognitive effort (44, 45).

text.text: Several limitations of our study should be acknowledged.
The design is crosssectional, which means developmental trajectories are inferred from age differences rather than individual change, and cohort effects cannot be ruled out.
In addition, our older adult sample is relatively modest in size, and the gap in coverage of middle age means the transition from young adulthood to older adulthood is not well characterized.
Longitudinal work with more uniform age sampling would be valuable to support and complement the findings of the current study.
These limitations notwithstanding, our results clearly demonstrate that exploration is neither a uniform behavior nor one with a unified developmental timeline.
How exploration changes with age -and what drives that change -critically depends on which component of exploration one examines, and in what motivational context people explore.
Our findings raise interesting questions that should be addressed in future research: Is random exploration really strategic exploitation?
Does high working memory (or fluid intelligence generally) protect against biases in uncertainty processing?
And might lifespan changes in strategic exploration be tied to lifespan changes in the value of information for current life goals?
There is plenty yet to explore.
